summary:
MicroFlame is an interactive tool for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, "Flame in Freefall". It shows what NASA knows about fire in microgravity, how well that knowledge applies to future spacecraft, and where there is no data.

We merged 1,372 test records from NASA's PSI repository (Saffire I-III, BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME) into one clean table. Missing values stay empty and every row carries a data-quality note. On top of it we built a simulator: choose a material and an environment (Earth, Moon, Mars or open space), set oxygen, pressure and airflow, and see the closest real experiments with their sources, or an honest "no data". A 3D cabin, labeled as an illustration, shows how gravity changes flame and smoke, using NASA fact-sheet gravity values.

The key finding is a gap. Future cabins are planned with lower pressure and more oxygen (8.2 psia, 34% O₂), yet solid materials in our data were tested only near 1 atm and up to about 22.7% O₂, and the PSI data we used has no direct measurements at lunar or Martian gravity.

MicroFlame is not a fire predictor: it maps evidence and gaps to help researchers and mission planners choose the next experiments. Its AI assistant answers only from the supplied data.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
MicroFlame turns NASA microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight. You pick a material and an environment (Earth, Moon, Mars or open space), set oxygen, pressure and airflow, and it shows the closest real NASA experiments with their sources, or an honest “no data”. It is not a fire predictor.
Under the hood, Python adapters read each PSI investigation (Saffire I–III, BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME) and merge them into one table of 1,372 records with 62 fields. A matching engine finds tests within ±2 percentage points of O₂ and ±10% of pressure (“same conditions”) or ±5 points and ±25% (“nearby”), and returns a verdict (data exist, few, indirect, none) in plain language with the PSI id and test id. A fact base of 51 sourced items (NASA ISS combustion guide, NASA-STD-6001, partial-gravity literature, ESA/JAXA/ZARM) adds context with page numbers.

What benefits does it have?
Researchers see which conditions were tested and which were not. Mission planners see that planned cabin atmospheres (8.2 psia, 34% O₂) lie outside the tested range for solid materials, which were tested only near 1 atm and up to about 22.7% O₂. Students and the public get plain-language answers instead of raw tables. Every number is traceable to a source.

What is the intended impact?
To help decide which experiments to run next, make the limits of today’s evidence visible before crews rely on it, and make microgravity fire research easier to understand and verify.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
Python (data pipeline), JavaScript, HTML and CSS (site and matching engine), Three.js (3D cabin), esbuild (bundling), Playwright (automated testing and screenshots), and Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and research assistant. Data: NASA PSI repository, NASA fact sheets, NASA documents. No special hardware is needed; it runs in a web browser.

How is it creative?
Instead of predicting fire, it maps the gaps in evidence. Slider ranges that NASA never tested are striped, and the tool refuses to answer outside tested conditions. A 3D cabin changes with the environment: gravity from NASA fact sheets (Moon 1.62 m/s², Mars 3.73 m/s², open space 0) changes how objects, smoke and flame look. It is clearly labeled as an illustration, because no speed or time is calculated.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Data quality: we never invent values; missing data stay empty, every row has a quality note, planned and measured values are kept apart.
  • Honesty: no extrapolation, sources and page numbers on every fact, “full text read” or “abstract only” labels.
  • Missing evidence: the PSI data used has no direct measurements at lunar or Martian gravity, so those environments are marked “indirect”.
  • Real cabin conditions: ventilation matters (flame spread is strongest near about 10 cm/s), and future atmospheres have more oxygen and lower pressure.
  • Reproducibility: one script rebuilds the whole dataset.
  • Usability and performance: plain language, a fallback panel when 3D is unavailable, and adjustable quality for slower devices.
